0d399303-e091-5249-87cf-68e9ac89a080.title: Royal Art and Architecture
0d399303-e091-5249-87cf-68e9ac89a080.description: In 1130, the newly crowned King of Sicily, Ruggero II, began to commission courtly art in which Islamic and Byzantine influences were added to the existing Romanic-Norman elements of local art and architecture. This process was compounded by Ruggero II's successful campaigns in the coastal territories of North Africa and the Byzantine Balkan Peninsula, with their consequent forced appropriation of workers. This gave rise to a recognisable form of royal art and architecture that made it possible to identify secular and religious works commissioned by the crown.
0d399303-e091-5249-87cf-68e9ac89a080.quote: *'Ruggero II commissioned courtly art in which Islamic and Byzantine influences were added to existing Romanic-Norman elements.'*

119ab24b-479f-5ff2-b732-0ff4c64e08e5.title: Islamicised Communities Before and After the Norman Conquest
119ab24b-479f-5ff2-b732-0ff4c64e08e5.description: Everyday and funerary objects such as terracotta jars with funerary inscriptions, some of which are similar to certain North African pieces, whether produced by craftsmen based on the island or imported from North Africa or the Muslim areas of the Iberian peninsula, bear witness to the long-lasting relationships between different Mediterranean regions that managed to bridge the divide between two opposing worlds until well into the 14th century.
119ab24b-479f-5ff2-b732-0ff4c64e08e5.quote: *'Everyday objects are evidence of the long-lasting relations between different Mediterranean regions.'*

1de88509-41c2-5db1-91f2-cf64dc633e29.title: Christian Sicily and Islamic Figurative Culture: Foundations and Continuity

5d8d84b8-9df4-5581-af50-feecdace83f5.title: Islamicised Communities Before and After the Norman Conquest
5d8d84b8-9df4-5581-af50-feecdace83f5.description: The Arab period in Sicily survived for a considerable time in the form of domestic and social customs, as well as in the use of places linked to rituals and practices dating back to the time the island was under Islamic rule. The survival, mainly in smaller towns, of fragments of urban fabric that are similar to examples found in North Africa, despite the differences between their respective architectural contexts, bear witness to the legacy of the Islamic presence on the island's urban landscape.
5d8d84b8-9df4-5581-af50-feecdace83f5.quote: *'The Arab period in Sicily survived for a considerable time in the form of social customs.'*

6780505e-c91f-5e51-8a78-74d186fc4a0b.title: Islamicised Communities Before and After the Norman Conquest
6780505e-c91f-5e51-8a78-74d186fc4a0b.description: The adoption in less fertile areas of irrigation and farming techniques based on a knowledge of the ancient world, along with other hydraulic engineering projects of Iranian origin (such as the impressive network of *qanat*), were some of the more remarkable aspects of land organisation during the period of Islamic rule.
6780505e-c91f-5e51-8a78-74d186fc4a0b.quote: *'Farming and irrigation techniques were some of the more remarkable aspects of land organisation.'*

6ca7f36b-6ff1-5be2-b8a1-162095f62272.title: Royal Art and Architecture
6ca7f36b-6ff1-5be2-b8a1-162095f62272.description: The religious architecture of the Norman court can be seen in a number of churches that were built around existing structures from the Islamic period.
6ca7f36b-6ff1-5be2-b8a1-162095f62272.quote: *'Some royal Norman churches were built on the remains of Islamic sites.'*

7bb30298-992c-56ba-a331-b96f90384fbb.title: Christian Sicily and Islamic Figurative Culture: Foundations and Continuity
7bb30298-992c-56ba-a331-b96f90384fbb.description: Paradoxically, it was the Christian kingdom of the Normans that left Sicily with some of the most valuable examples of Islamic art to be found in the Mediterranean basin, albeit with the addition of classical, Byzantine and Iranian elements. Instead of seeking to antagonise its predecessors, the new dynasty consciously assimilated Islamic culture and customs, looking to the contemporary Muslim world for the refined culture that it could offer. Contact between the cultures was not limited to Muslims who had remained on the island, but most notably extended to the relationship between the Norman court and the Fatimid Caliphate of Cairo, which is evident from diplomatic and commercial relations and even in the exchange of gifts, such as those between Caliph al-Hafiz (r. 1131–49) and Ruggero II. It is highly likely that some of the craftsmen employed in the royal Norman workshops came from Egypt.
7bb30298-992c-56ba-a331-b96f90384fbb.quote: *'It was the Normans that left Sicily with some of the most valuable examples of Islamic art.'*

87981465-ac17-588c-98d9-d4f2d4298bdc.title: The Normans in Sicily
87981465-ac17-588c-98d9-d4f2d4298bdc.description: 'The Arabs left the Norman kingdom of Sicily a cultural heritage and civilisation whose Greek, Latin and Byzantine roots helped to sow the first seeds of the Italian Renaissance.'

extra.intro_text:
Occupied from AD 827 by the armies of the *amir* of Kairouan, Sicily was part of the Islamic world until 1061, although some staunch pockets of Greco-Byzantine resistance in the east of the island managed to hold out until 965.  
Despite limited immigration from North Africa, the Iberian peninsula, Egypt and the Middle East, the social structures of Islam were established and spread quickly. During these two centuries of Arabic presence, Qur'anic law guaranteed profession of the Christian faith, although not without discrimination.  
In 1061 the Normans, led by the Altavilla family, landed on the island from their bases in Southern Italy. In 1094, Roger I (Ruggero d'Altavilla, r. 1098–1101) established the County of Sicily, which was inherited by his son Roger II (Ruggero II d'Altavilla, r. 1112 as count; king 1130–54). His successors William I (Guglielmo I, r. 1154–66) and William II (Guglielmo II, r. 1171–89) continued his aggressive policy towards Muslims, Byzantium and the Holy Roman Empire before the succession of the Swabian dynasty in 1194.  
Just as they had during the period of Arab rule, the Christian and Muslim communities existed side by side, ensuring the survival of social rituals and customs from the Islamic period, evident in particular in the new Christian dynasty's re-use of sites and buildings valued by the previous rulers.  
This cultural continuity was reinforced by ongoing political relations between the Normans and the Islamic world. One of the most emblematic expressions of these relations was the marked desire of the Norman dynasty, once the Kingdom of Sicily had been established, to reshape Sicilian art using models derived from Islamic art, which were consciously added to existing, modest Siculo-Arabian and Byzantine forms in art and architecture.  
The result was a proactive syncretism that made Siculo-Norman art one of the most original in medieval Europe and the Mediterranean.

8d71ce09-ebae-530f-ab2a-0c71746f1822.title: Islamicised Communities Before and After the Norman Conquest

d56f34dd-618b-52fd-941d-524f966fe3d5.title: Royal Art and Architecture
d56f34dd-618b-52fd-941d-524f966fe3d5.description: The ability to borrow typological and figurative solicitations from Islamic and Byzantine art (with a certain openness to a wide range of different influences, including of Sassanian origin) gave the art arising from the 'politics of the image' used by the Norman kings a proactive and highly original syncretism.
d56f34dd-618b-52fd-941d-524f966fe3d5.quote: *'The “politics of the image” used by the Norman kings made extensive use of Islamic artistic models.'*

e7b309d4-f6ec-5a3c-85a4-64bb13cff1d3.title: Islamicised Communities Before and After the Norman Conquest
e7b309d4-f6ec-5a3c-85a4-64bb13cff1d3.description: There is very little material evidence of the period of Islamic rule in Sicily, this term being understood to cover both the time the entire island was governed by the Kalbid *amir*s (who were Fatimid subjects) and the Norman conquest, during which a few areas remained in the hands of the Muslims for a limited time. In architecture, this evidence often consists of masonry remains of mosques and fortresses, usually incorporated into later structures.
e7b309d4-f6ec-5a3c-85a4-64bb13cff1d3.quote: '*There is very little material evidence of Islamic rule in Sicily, consisting mainly of masonry remains.'*

f4035718-d69a-5c0e-b8cf-7d6e57c6114f.title: Christian Sicily and Islamic Figurative Culture: Foundations and Continuity
f4035718-d69a-5c0e-b8cf-7d6e57c6114f.description: The influence of Islamic artistic culture as adopted by the Normans was still evident in a series of exquisite objects produced in the following (13th) century, including several refined ivory pieces.
f4035718-d69a-5c0e-b8cf-7d6e57c6114f.quote: *'The influence of Islamic artistic culture was still evident in objects produced in the following century.'*

f70d4425-5bc1-5d34-bbc8-8c1e22ee9757.title: Royal Art and Architecture
f70d4425-5bc1-5d34-bbc8-8c1e22ee9757.description: The establishment of the *tiraz* workshop, a royal atelier for the production of precious artefacts and fabrics near the Royal Palace, was an important vehicle for the spread of figurative repertoires and manufacturing techniques in Islamic culture.
f70d4425-5bc1-5d34-bbc8-8c1e22ee9757.quote: *'The* tiraz *workshop* *was an important vehicle for the spread of figurative repertoires.'*
